metadata.file_name: Predictors of reading performance of fourth-grade Turkish students[#1688295]-4824605.pdf
metadata.title: Predictors of reading performance of fourth-grade Turkish students

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 microdata for fourth-grade students in Türkiye, merged from student, teacher, home, and school questionnaires. The manuscript describes preprocessing (purging cases with >20% missing data, k-nearest-neighbor mean imputation with k=10, and centering/variance scaling) and then trains an SVM classifier on a binary high/low reading performance indicator derived from PIRLS ASRIBM01 (first plausible value). However, it does not report whether PIRLS sampling/survey weights or replicate weights were applied in model training or evaluation. Because the analysis is an SVM-based ML pipeline, the paper does not specify any weight-aware estimation; therefore, readers should treat the results as conditional on the modeling choices and note that population-representative inference may require applying PIRLS complex-sample weights (and appropriate variance estimation) if available in the dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2021 openly accessible dataset (pirls2021.org/data) and constructed an analytic file by merging student, teacher, home, and school questionnaires via an R script. The consolidated raw file contained 6032 students; cases with more than 20% missing data were removed, reducing the sample to 5538. Remaining missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbor mean imputation (k=10). From the initial 545 variables, the author manually retained 405 independent variables deemed potentially relevant for reading success. The dependent outcome was converted to a binary identifier using ASRIBM01 (benchmark score of the first plausible value), recoding the lowest two categories as low performance and the highest two categories as high performance, yielding 3589 students (1799 low, 1790 high).

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Türkiye Grade 4 Reading (ASRIBM01 first plausible value; binary high vs low)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (linear kernel, L2-regularized) — Accuracy: 0.957 (95% CI: 0.943–0.968); Kappa: 0.914; Sensitivity/Recall: 0.956; Specificity: 0.958; Balanced Accuracy: 0.9572; PPV: 0.956; NPV: 0.958; P-value [Acc > NIR] < 0.001. Feature selection via RFE with 5x repeated 10-fold CV; best subset reported as top 16 factors (vs 4/8/405).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Türkiye Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged emphasis on foundational literacy instruction (letter-sound and alphabet knowledge), access to take-home books, assessment practices (e.g., observing students as they work), and parental commitment to learning readiness to predict whether students were in the high- vs low-reading performance class, finding that the SVM achieved 95.7% accuracy with high agreement (Kappa=0.914). This indicates that strengthening school-level instructional emphasis on early reading skills, combined with interactive assessment practices and family readiness support, may improve the proportion of students reaching higher reading performance levels, though the results are predictive and causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional PIRLS data.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading data for Türkiye, using ASRIBM01 (the benchmark score of the first plausible value) recoded into a binary high- vs low-performance indicator. After merging questionnaire files, the author purged cases with >20% missingness, imputed remaining missing values using k-nearest-neighbor mean imputation (k=10), and normalized features (centering and variance scaling). A linear, L2-regularized SVM was trained with 5-times repeated 10-fold cross-validation, with a 70/30 train-test split (training n=2513; test n=1076). The best model used the top 16 factors selected via recursive feature elimination, yielding Accuracy=0.957 (95% CI 0.943–0.968), Kappa=0.914, sensitivity=0.956, specificity=0.958, and balanced accuracy=0.9572 (P<0.001 vs no-information rate). The paper does not report the use of PIRLS sampling/replicate weights, and the outcome is a predictive classification rather than a causal estimate.
